notes:
I've written notes on all 22 verses except v. 43, where I found no comment specific to that verse. Most of the material comes from the older commentaries (Gill, Matthew Henry, Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch, Calvin, Clarke, Poole) and from David Guzik (Enduring Word). Some gaps to know about:

- **Searches cut short.** I ran out of searches and page fetches. The full-chapter pages for the Pulpit Commentary and Gill only loaded up to around v. 31 and v. 19, and the Ellicott chapter page didn't load at all. So for vv. 34–44 I'm relying on search summaries.
- **No NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey.** I didn't get to either. The textual and "scholarly" notes below come from older critical commentators (Pulpit, Keil & Delitzsch).
- **Few modern denominational sources.** I found nothing from Lutheran, Methodist, Pentecostal or Anglican teachers, or from catholic.com or oca.org. The only "tradition" contrast I found is v. 33, and it's a difference of emphasis rather than a real split.
- **No prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace material.** Nothing I found discusses this passage in connection with those movements.

---

**v. 23**
- Guzik (Enduring Word): Each dawning day gives mankind hope in fresh mercies and compassions from God. We need a constant supply and God has promised to send them without fail. Even in the disaster God was faithful. He announced his judgments and carried them out, and he would keep his promise of restoration just as faithfully. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Guzik, quoting Ryken: the prophet turns to speak to God directly ("*your* faithfulness"), and in the process of remembering God's attributes, Jeremiah was drawn back into living fellowship and intimate communion with his faithful God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Matthew Henry: the covenant seemed broken, but the people admitted it was still in force. Whatever hard things we suffer, we must never entertain any hard thoughts of God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_003.cfm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: Our wants are constant; so is the Divine provision. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
- Text note (Pulpit): v. 23 is clearly parallel to v. 22, where the subject is "the LORD's mercies" rather than "we". So the Pulpit prefers the ancient Targum and Syriac reading of v. 22, "they cease not", over "we are not consumed". https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm

**v. 24**
- Guzik: as in Psalm 119:57, Jeremiah found satisfaction by making the LORD his portion. Whatever his share or future would be, it would be found in Yahweh. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/ Guzik also says God couldn't really be his hope until he was first his portion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm
- Spurgeon's devotional (reproduced on Precept Austin): the verse doesn't say the Lord is *partly* my portion. He himself is the whole of the soul's inheritance, not His grace merely, nor His love, nor His covenant, but Jehovah Himself! https://www.preceptaustin.org/a_powerful_principle_hope_in_god
- Pulpit: the line echoes Psalm 16:5 (compare Psalms 73:26, 119:57, 142:5). https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Matthew Henry (Concise): earthly portions perish, but God is a portion for ever. If we can't yet say "The Lord is my portion" firmly, we can at least say we want him to be. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm

**v. 25**
- Guzik: Judah's misery came because they would not truly seek God and wait for him. They rebelled for generations and looked to others to rescue them. Seeking him again would bring fresh experience of his goodness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Precept Austin (devotional): those who hope in the Lord can expect His goodness (Lamentations 3:25). https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries

**v. 26**
- Pulpit: better rendered "wait in silence". In the Psalms, silence expresses resignation to God's will (Psalms 62:1, 65:1). The thought matches Psalm 37:7. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: there should be no striving or crying out. Confidence in His power to save hushes fears and doubts. Complaining only makes suffering harder to bear. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
- Guzik quotes an older writer: hoping and waiting are like mother and daughter, and all turbulency and impatience of spirit under sad providences is opposed to waiting. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm

**v. 27**
- Guzik: hard seasons are sometimes better faced young. If God disciplines us when we are young, it is to train us for a fruitful future. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm
- Clarke (Methodist): Early habits, when good, are invaluable. Early discipline is equally so. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-27.html
- Barnes: someone who suffers early learns silent endurance in good time, which makes calm patience easier later in life. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-27.html
- Matthew Henry: many of Judah's young men had been carried into captivity, and the verse encouraged them to accept it. It can also be applied to taking up the yoke of God's commands while young. But here it seems to be meant of the yoke of affliction. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/lamentations/3.htm
- Pulpit: youth is named because that's when people adapt and accept discipline most easily. The verse doesn't prove the writer was young. The reading "*from* his youth", found in the Vulgate and some manuscripts, is in the Pulpit's view probably a scribal change made to support Jeremiah as author. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary agrees the writer may have been an older man looking back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
- Spurgeon preached on this verse ("The Best Burden for Young Shoulders"), noting that the illustration is drawn from cattle. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-best-burden-for-young-shoulders
- *Early church use:* Aphrahat, a 4th-century Syriac Church Father, applied vv. 27–28 to monks and virgins: whoever takes up the yoke of Christ should keep it pure and live alone. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/370106.htm

**v. 28**
- Pulpit: vv. 28–30 should be read as commands ("let him sit… let him keep silence"). Since affliction is good for a man, he should sit still and accept it when trouble comes. The phrase "because he hath borne it" is better read as "when he (God) hath laid it". https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Matthew Henry: we should stay silent under a yoke we didn't pull onto ourselves, patiently accepting it because God laid it on us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhcw/lamentations/3.htm
- Guzik: in hardship it's best not to try to work everything out at once. It's a time for reflection and listening rather than talking. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm
- Guzik, quoting another commentator: "Silence implies both an acceptance of God's will and a refusal to complain to men." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/

**v. 29**
- Pulpit: putting one's mouth in the dust was an Eastern way of showing submission (Micah 7:17; Psalm 72:9). https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch (citing Nägelsbach) see a rising scale in vv. 28–30. The sitting alone and in silence is comparatively the easiest; it is harder to place the mouth in the dust, and yet cling to hope. Hardest of all is offering the cheek to the one who strikes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm

**v. 30**
- Pulpit: the verse closely echoes Job 16:10. In these books the righteous person is marked by patient endurance of suffering, an ideal taken up and widened by Christ in Matthew 5:39. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: patiently bear insult from men, as Job did and as the Servant of the LORD did (Isaiah 50:6). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary also links the verse to the Sermon on the Mount and to "when reviled, not to revile again". https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
- Guzik: they should patiently accept the suffering and shame God had appointed. He quotes a commentator: "In offering the cheek to the smiter the captive was conveying the idea of absolute surrender." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm

**v. 31**
- Keil & Delitzsch: vv. 31–33 give the reasons for comfort. The first is that the sorrow will end, because the Lord does not cast off for ever. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm
- Pulpit's summary: the trouble lasts only for a time, and God will show compassion again. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-33.html
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: God's abandonment of His people is only temporary. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html

**v. 32**
- Keil & Delitzsch: after he causes sorrow, God shows pity again, out of the fullness of his grace. Compassion outweighs sorrow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm
- Ellicott: this comfort rests on the fact that compassion underlies chastisement (Psalms 30:5; Job 5:18; Isaiah 54:8). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-3.html
- Guzik: God caused grief in his wise judgments, but he also promised compassion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm

**v. 33** (the only verse where I found a contrast between traditions)
- Ellicott and Pulpit: "willingly" literally means "from the heart", the heart being the seat of will as well as feeling. https://biblehub.com/lamentations/3-33.htm Ellicott adds that God's first, eternal will is on the side of love, and punishment goes, as it were, against that will. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/lamentations-3.html
- **Reformed (Calvin):** this is a human way of speaking about God, since God never acts half-heartedly. His picture is a judge who willingly condemns the guilty because it's his duty, yet doesn't do it "from the heart", because he wishes everyone were innocent. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-33.html
- **Reformed/Baptist (Gill):** all afflictions come from God, but unlike his good gifts they don't come from his sovereign pleasure alone. Sin is their cause, and God sends them reluctantly and in love. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm Gill limits "children of men" here to those God has loved and made his sons. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-33.html
- **Geneva Bible (Calvinist):** God takes no pleasure in it but does it out of necessity, to correct us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm
- **Wesleyan/Arminian:** StudyLight quotes Wesley's Notes: "not from his own mere motion without a cause given him from the persons afflicted". https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-33.html Clarke (Methodist) compares God to a loving parent who uses the rod not to gratify himself, but to profit and save us. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/bsb/lamentations/3-33.html
- **How big is the difference?** StudyLight labels its commentators as splitting several ways on this verse. But the readings I saw largely agree that God afflicts reluctantly and because of sin. Poole, for example, sounds just like Wesley and adds that mercy is God's natural work while judgment is his "strange work". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm The real difference is in emphasis. Calvin stresses God's undivided will as judge, while Wesley and Clarke stress that the cause lies in the person and the aim is their good. Gill's narrowing to God's own children is distinctive. Note that in the Barnes notes, the phrase "much less the godly" applies the verse to all people. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/lamentations-3.html

**vv. 34–36**
- Gill gives two readings. Either God himself does none of these wrongs when he afflicts, or, his preferred reading, the lines connect to "the Lord approveth not": he doesn't approve of others treating captives cruelly or twisting justice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/lamentations/3.htm
- Coffman, citing the Pulpit, takes v. 34 as the Babylonians' cruelties, mentioned to show that God disapproves of human atrocities. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/lamentations/3-38.html
- Guzik, quoting Harrison on v. 35: the Hebrew supports the idea of rights a person has before God, and God strongly disapproves of taking those rights away in court. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: God doesn't afflict willingly, yet He is not indifferent to the injustice of man to man. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
- Swindoll (via Precept Austin) lists three violations God notices: mistreating prisoners (v. 34), denying basic rights (v. 35) and overturning justice (v. 36). https://www.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries
- Text note on v. 36 (Pulpit): "approveth not" depends on changing one letter. The Hebrew as written reads "the Lord seeth not". https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Keil & Delitzsch: vv. 34–39 make the point that every wrong on earth is under God's control. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-33.htm

**v. 37**
- Keil & Delitzsch: Nothing takes place on the earth which the Lord has not appointed; no man can give and execute a command against the will of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-37.htm Luther's free translation is "Who dares to say that such a thing happens without the command of the Lord?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm
- Guzik: God rules over everything, directly or by what he allows, and that sovereignty is a source of hope. It was and is worse to be at the mercy of blind fate. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/lamentations/lamentations-3.cfm

**v. 38**
- Poole: "evil" here means punishment and painful judgments, as in Job 2:10 and Amos 3:6. It's no insult to God to call him the author of his own punishments. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm
- Gill: this is not the evil of sin. God forbids sin and doesn't author it, though he allows it "by his permissive will" and overrules it for good. The "evils" are judgments and the chastening of his people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm
- Geneva Bible: "evil and good" means adversity and prosperity. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm
- Pulpit (Homiletics): the prophets rejected Persian dualism, the idea of a good power and an evil power. But they do not teach that moral evil is caused by God. The context shows suffering is meant, not sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/lamentations-3.html The same page warns that we must not assume no trouble can come to us if God is with us. Nor should we assume that if trouble comes, God cannot be with us. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/lamentations-3.html
- Biblical Illustrator (Adeney): the poet says "evil and good", not "good and evil". Good shall have the last word. https://biblehub.com/sermons/lamentations/3-38.htm

**v. 39**
- Keil & Delitzsch read it as: why does a man sigh as long as he lives? Let each one sigh for his sins. In other words, grieve over sin, not over suffering. Keil rejects the "in view of his sins" rendering (the one the BSB uses) as linguistically impossible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm
- Gill: a "living man" is kept alive by God and is not yet in hell, where he deserves to be, so he should praise rather than complain. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/lamentations/3.htm
- Thomas Brooks (Puritan, via Precept Austin): if we deserve damnation, we can't call God too severe for a fatherly whipping. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/lamentations_commentaries
- Matthew Henry (Concise): what we complain of is far less than our sins deserve. We should complain to God, and not of him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm
- Adeney adds a caution: some suffering is not punishment, the cry of suffering children for example. https://biblehub.com/sermons/lamentations/3-38.htm

**v. 40**
- Guzik: even while feeling God as an enemy, Jeremiah recommended humble self-examination. But self-examination does little good unless it leads us back to the LORD. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: the wording implies going all the way back, not half way. A repentance that spends itself in emotions and tears is ineffective. Sorrow for sin is but a symptom of repentance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
- Matthew Henry (Concise): in hard times we tend to blame others, but our duty is to examine our own ways. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm

**v. 41**
- Matthew Henry (Concise): Our hearts must go with our prayers. If inward impressions do not answer to outward expressions, we mock God, and deceive ourselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/lamentations/3-38.htm

**v. 42**
- Preacher's Homiletical Commentary: a sight of God throws light on a person's past, and in that light people are forced to judge themselves as God does. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/lamentations-3.html
- Gill's outline: from v. 42 comes a prayer confessing sin and mourning their misery, because God has hidden his face and enemies mock them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/lamentations/3.htm
- Guzik: to turn back, they had to see their condition honestly. They were under God's severe discipline because of deep and persistent sin. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/lamentations-3/

**v. 44**
- Pulpit (in its note on v. 8, which it links to v. 44): a kind of barrier that unanswered prayers cannot get through. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/lamentations/3.htm
- Gill (on v. 8, referring to v. 44): the rabbi Jarchi (Rashi) read it as the windows of heaven being shut so prayer can't pass through. Gill takes it as God's disregard, or apparent disregard, of the people's prayer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/lamentations/3.htm
- Matthew Henry: The prolonging of troubles is sometimes a temptation, even to praying people, to question whether God be what they have always believed him to be, a prayer-hearing God. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lam/Lam_003.cfm
